arxiv:2611.06728.text: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit. From Shuai Dong and colleagues. Streaming video models must decide at each moment whether to answer or keep watching. Existing training methods often give every decision the same credit for the whole interaction, which can reward repeated answers or penalize useful follow-ups. TurnWise assigns credit separately to each decision and gives answering and waiting decisions equal weight, without needing a learned critic or extra trials. Experiments show it performs better than earlier reinforcement learning methods for understanding streaming video.

arxiv:2611.05193.text: Factorized MLLM Embeddings for Composed Image Retrieval. From WonJun Moon and colleagues. Composed image retrieval must find an image that matches a reference image after a text-described change. Existing methods can turn the image and text into a retrieval representation without clearly working out the intended change. FactEmbed uses separate internal representations to imagine the target image, then trains them to support retrieval and reranking. Across composed image retrieval benchmarks, it outperforms prior methods, while producing the representations needed for reranking in the same model pass.

arxiv:2611.06483.text: What Does Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning Really Improve in LLM Agents? From Kejian Zhu and colleagues. Multi-turn reinforcement learning can help language model agents on long tasks, but its gains may depend on how many interactions they get. The study evaluates performance across different numbers of attempts and conversation turns, and finds that gains shrink when turn budgets are tight. The method does not consistently improve single-step decisions; its main strengths are recovering from errors and staying effective over long tasks. A training approach called BudgetMix varies interaction budgets and performs robustly across different execution settings.

arxiv:2611.06741.text: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing. From Ruikang Li and colleagues. Repeated image edits can gradually change parts of an image that should stay the same, even when each edit works well on its own. TailSteer is a final-stage training method that preserves the model's early image-generation process and teaches it to correct unwanted changes near the end. It learns from the model's own editing runs, using unchanged image content as a guide rather than curated examples. Across three model families, it reduced drift over fifteen to twenty editing turns while largely preserving performance on image creation and single-edit tasks.

arxiv:2611.06518.text: EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL. From Mingzhe Zheng and colleagues. Emotional expression in generated videos is hard to score because there is no single correct answer, and fixed rewards can miss intent or encourage reward hacking. EmoReward plans visible cues from the prompt, scores the video with different signals, and adjusts how much each signal matters based on the scene. It also learns which signals proved reliable during one training run and uses that evidence to calibrate the next, without changing the reward models. Tests report improvements across several training methods, with further support from studies on other image-generation models.

arxiv:2611.06425.text: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding. From Baoyou Chen and colleagues. Speculative decoding can be slow when each draft of candidate tokens must wait for the target model to finish checking the previous draft. D3D is a standalone diffusion drafter that predicts successor blocks without needing updated target-model states, so drafting can overlap with verification. It also removes layers that contribute little to the length of accepted drafts. Across seven benchmarks, D3D achieves higher average speedups than DFlash with both tested target models.

arxiv:2611.06918.text: From Pixels to Actions, Towards Native Vision-Language-Action Policies. From Weichen Fan and colleagues. Vision-language-action systems often compress an image into a fixed representation before reasoning about what to do. NEO-VLA instead lets image patches and language evolve together through the model, so its action planner can use visual information from different depths. In controlled comparisons, this design outperforms systems built around fixed visual encoders, and the advantage remains after fine-tuning or adding scale. It also delivers stronger, more robust control across manipulation tasks and shifts in conditions.

arxiv:2611.06910.text: FrontierPhysics: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Physics Research. From Bingran You and colleagues. Physics benchmarks often test fixed questions or narrow tasks, leaving the quality of full research work unchecked. FrontierPhysics brings together fifty-six research tasks from theoretical, computational, and experimental physics, asking agents to review prior work, plan and conduct research, and write scientific reports. Across twenty-two models tested in twenty-six configurations, none passed more than forty-six of one hundred sixty-eight attempts. Reviews suggest the main limits are weak reasoning and expert judgment, not missing physics knowledge or execution mistakes.

arxiv:2611.06796.text: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation. From Yihong Luo and colleagues. Few-step diffusion models can generate images and videos quickly, but keeping their quality high with only a few steps is difficult. VA-TDM uses a learned critic to compare how the student and teacher models move through generation, providing feedback across intermediate steps. Tests show state-of-the-art results for four-step text-to-image and text-to-video generation across several model families, with the method scaling to a thirty-three-billion-parameter model. Human preferences also favored its outputs over Fast-H3 and found them closer to the original many-step model.

arxiv:2611.05648.text: NitroFusion2: Bringing Adversarial Loss to the Text Stream of Multimodal Diffusion Transformers. From Dar-Yen Chen and colleagues. Adversarial distillation usually judges generated images using image features, but multimodal diffusion transformers also have a text stream that absorbs information from the image. NitroFusion2 uses those text-token states to guide training, and lets a discriminator focus on aspects such as typography, objects, or style. It brings generation down from the usual four to eight steps to one or two at comparable quality. At one step, it produces sharp text and fine detail, making very fast image generation practical.

arxiv:2611.05163.text: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On. From Seungyong Lee and colleagues. Adapting robot policies to new tasks often requires costly teleoperated demonstrations. RoboTryOn turns human videos into videos of a target robot, keeping the demonstrated motion, objects, and background while replacing the person with the robot. It then infers robot actions from the generated video to train a policy. Across several humanoid robots, synthetic training data raised average success on novel tasks from two percent to sixty percent, including difficult two-handed tasks, without real demonstrations of those tasks.

arxiv:2611.06083.text: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding? From Peiran Wu and colleagues. Video models often combine sampled frames and audio, but it is unclear whether they need to hear audio directly to understand a clip. SleuthVLM uses a vision-language model that reads speech transcripts and investigates the video without a fixed workflow. Across four benchmarks, it reaches the best average accuracy at seventy-five percent, and leads the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard at seventy-seven point eight percent. The results suggest that stronger agent skills may matter more than direct audio input or more training to align audio and video.

arxiv:2611.05988.text: LiveFoley: Dynamic Real-Time Video-to-Audio Generation for Immersive Interactive Worlds. From Yusheng Dai and colleagues. Real-time video-to-audio generation must keep sounds aligned with changing visuals without sacrificing audio quality. LiveFoley tackles this by adapting a visual encoder to stream with a sliding window, and by letting its audio generator use context from earlier audio. It can also trade a small amount of look-ahead for more quality. Experiments show that LiveFoley matches offline models in timing and produces better audio than other streaming systems.

arxiv:2611.05593.text: GaussianRenderFormer: Transformer-based Rendering of 3D Gaussian Splats. From Shahaf Valencia Levy and colleagues. Rendering three-dimensional Gaussian splats usually relies on a rasterizer, and this work asks whether a neural network can produce the image directly instead. GaussianRenderFormer encodes each Gaussian as a token, then uses a camera-aware decoder to turn patches of viewing rays into pixels. On three hundred unseen objects, it reached thirty-eight point zero eight decibels in peak signal-to-noise ratio, compared with forty-four point zero two for rasterizing the same pruned splats. Supplying the decoder with each Gaussian's projected footprint improved its score by one point four decibels, pointing to the decoder as a possible bottleneck.

arxiv:2611.05609.text: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation. From Yichen Wang and colleagues. On-policy distillation can look successful on familiar tasks while failing to transfer teachers' ability to handle new or combined tasks. Tests across math, coding, agents, and long-context tasks found that distilled models often matched teachers on familiar examples but lagged on unfamiliar ones. The gap shrank when the work addressed both teacher capability and gaps in training data. The study also introduces ways to improve unfamiliar-task performance while largely retaining familiar-task results.

arxiv:2611.06817.text: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models. From Juncheng Ma and colleagues. Robot learning can benefit from human videos, but turning large video collections into reliable robot skills requires careful data and training methods. Open-HumanScale provides an open recipe and a curated collection of fifty thousand hours of video, annotated with hand motion and language. The researchers find that more pretraining data is linked to higher robot success, and show that combining human and robot experience improves results, including success rates of 92.70 percent on one simulation task and 84.60 percent on a more varied version. On physical robots, the model also adapts to new visual goals without being retrained.

arxiv:2611.06768.text: PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World. From Qiang Wang and colleagues. Robot coding agents can turn spatial reasoning into actions, but it is unclear how real-world experience can lead to lasting improvements in their abilities. PyRUA-REAL lets agents explore with a physical robot, refine code using execution feedback, and save experience as reusable skills and persistent memory. Across eight real-world tasks, it achieved an average success rate of 91.1 percent, and reached 84.4 percent on 42 RoboDojo benchmark tasks. The results show how physical exploration can build skills that support more robust and efficient robot behavior.

arxiv:2611.06042.text: UniRestorer++: Scalable Universal Image Restoration with Multi-Granularity Degradation Modeling. From Jingbo Lin and colleagues. Universal image restoration tries to remove many kinds of image damage with one model, but simply making models larger can stop improving results, and incorrect damage estimates can hurt performance. UniRestorer++ grows its capacity by grouping degradation types and assigning specialized experts, with routing that can adapt to both the image and local regions. The team also introduces a benchmark covering fifty degradation categories. Tests show steady gains as model size grows, stronger scaling on unfamiliar and real-world images, and leading results across benchmarks.

arxiv:2611.04527.text: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models. From Jaehyeong Jo and colleagues. Robot action models can benefit from video models, but generating future videos takes time and can produce errors that hurt control. DreamFree distills a pretrained video model's predictive knowledge into visual features computed from the current view, then uses those features to predict actions. Across simulated and real-world tasks, it achieves higher success rates than leading alternatives and runs closed-loop control at eleven hertz with a fourteen-billion-parameter video model. It can also learn new tasks from video demonstrations without action labels.

arxiv:2611.06908.text: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation. From Siyuan Hu and colleagues. Humanoid robots need examples linking what they see and hear to joint movements, but collecting these examples with people is slow. HALO creates vision and language paired with motion data in a thousand simulated homes, using computing power rather than human labor to scale the collection. It learns skills such as crawling under tables and pushing boxes, then combines them for longer tasks. Without training in real homes, it succeeds in 91 percent of 360 trials across six unfamiliar real-world environments.

arxiv:2611.06524.text: Distributed Consensus, Optimization, and Learning under Communication Constraints. From Zheng Chen and colleagues. Distributed optimization lets networked devices work together toward a shared goal, but their results depend on how well they exchange information. This tutorial explains consensus averaging and distributed optimization, then shows how network structure and uncertain communication affect cooperation and performance. It also reviews ways to make distributed learning more communication-efficient, especially over wireless networks. The work highlights the need to connect theory more closely with practice to realize the potential of networked intelligence.

arxiv:2611.06706.text: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus. From Tianwei Zhang and colleagues. Online abuse detection tools are built mostly around Global North languages, leaving many forms of gender-based harm under-recognized elsewhere. Working with civil society groups in Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, researchers gathered and annotated examples in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. Their ALTO dataset contains three thousand and twenty-two examples, and tests found existing models often missed this abuse, especially covert harms and content in Swahili. Fine-tuning improved detection, and the team released the dataset, annotation guide, and trained models.

arxiv:2611.06055.text: Softmax Attention with Any Temperature in Fixed Dimension: Matching the Best Known Maximum-Inner-Product Bounds. From Zixuan Huang and colleagues at Peking University. Direct attention compares every query with every key, making long contexts costly. This work gives a faster method in any fixed dimension, with an error-controlled running time and only polylogarithmic dependence on the input magnitudes and accuracy. For equal numbers of queries and keys, it is near-linear in dimensions two and three, and improves the known bounds in higher dimensions. Its guarantees hold for any positive temperature, and its running time matches the best known bounds for batch maximum-inner-product search.

arxiv:2611.06585.text: Signed, Sealed, Leaked: Trust Beyond Signature for MCP Toolchains. From Yichiet Aun and colleagues at Universiti Tunku Abdul Rahman. Signed software can still hide code that leaks private information, even when a runtime defence blocks direct attacks. This work tests a malicious Model Context Protocol tool and introduces germline execution, which runs each tool call in a separate copy that receives only information approved for its destination. Under stated assumptions, the authors prove that these copies limit what a tool can reveal. Across one hundred fifty-three attack runs, germline execution detected no unauthorised disclosures, while baseline methods and an ablation did so in five point nine to seventy-four point five percent of runs.

arxiv:2611.06696.text: You Know What You Will Like: People Predict Their Own Ratings Better Than Recommender Systems. From Zihan Chen and colleagues. Recommender systems infer what people will like from past ratings, but direct questions are often ignored. In a movie study, researchers compared people's forecasts for unseen films with four machine predictions, using only forecasts that were followed by a rating. People predicted their own ratings more accurately, and adding their forecast cut prediction error by twenty-six percent. Machines matched people when ranking their own movies, and did as well or better for older films with many ratings.

arxiv:2611.06690.text: System-Theoretic Analysis of Extended Cellular Potts Models for Tumor Invasion. From Andrea Tramaloni and colleagues. Modeling tumor invasion through tissue is difficult when tumor cells move along changing gradients in the extracellular matrix. This work gives extended Cellular Potts models a system-theoretic foundation by linking stochastic cell interactions with a mathematical description of matrix degradation. The analysis establishes bounds on transition probabilities and shows when the system converges. For one-dimensional cases, it also derives invasion-time probabilities, showing how invasion time depends on matrix gradients, cell number, and cells' tendency to keep a target volume.

arxiv:2611.06665.text: To lift or not to lift: Operator inference for nonlinear PDEs with boundary control. From Zhuoyuan Wang and colleagues. Boundary actuation can change which solutions a partial differential equation allows, a feature standard operator inference does not explicitly capture. This work tests a lifting-based approach that separates the part of the solution needed to satisfy changing boundary conditions from the part learned from data. In experiments on heat flow, Burgers' equation, and cavity flow, the method satisfies boundary conditions by construction and can improve prediction accuracy, stability, and computational efficiency. The gains vary, and standard operator inference can still work well in some cases.

arxiv:2611.05918.text: Autonomous ETL Pipelines for Salesforce M and A Consolidation: A Reference Framework, Jitterbit Mapping, and Reproducible Simulation Study. From Imran Basha Shaik and colleagues. Combining Salesforce systems during a merger is difficult because customer records may use different fields, contain duplicates, and change before cutover. The proposed framework automates data extraction, mapping, quality checks, duplicate matching, loading, and ongoing updates, with each stage tied to Jitterbit tools. In simulations, quality checks prevented load failures and lost picklist values, while incremental updates matched a full rebuild on more than 99.3 percent of field values. The framework still needs validation in a live deployment.

arxiv:2611.05970.text: Ray-Tracing-Based Dynamic Channel Sounding With Autoregressive Wi-Fi CSI Prediction. From Lyutianyang Zhang and colleagues. Mobile Wi-Fi devices can make channel information go stale, while frequent measurements use time and resources. This work combines ray tracing with a Transformer that predicts channel information from device positions, then selects how often to measure while accounting for prediction errors and overhead. In Wi-Fi seven simulations, beamforming with predicted channel information raised mean goodput over stale information by 67.3 percent on a linear path, 112.7 percent on a circular path, and 119.1 percent on a cosine path.

arxiv:2611.06859.text: Balancing hierarchical representation and quantization: A performance trade-off in text embeddings. From Kai Ponel and colleagues at Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Text embeddings can be made cheaper by shortening their representations or storing them at lower precision, but the effects of combining these approaches are not well understood. This benchmark tests both methods across thirty-eight tasks and four embedding models, measuring storage and evaluation time separately. Eight-bit quantization largely preserves performance, while binary quantization performs significantly worse across all task categories. Combining eightfold dimension reduction with eight-bit quantization cuts storage thirty-twofold while retaining 94.4 percent of baseline effectiveness.

arxiv:2611.05446.text: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model. From Dylan Herman and colleagues. Approximating the maximum energy in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model has been possible at fixed accuracy, but the work could grow too quickly as accuracy improves, and guarantees at finite size were missing. This work introduces a method that groups steps of an existing algorithm and uses exact Gaussian query outputs. It achieves a relative error of at most the requested accuracy using work that grows polynomially with both problem size and accuracy, with a finite-size guarantee above a stated dimension threshold. It also gives an asymptotic approximation scheme with an additive error independent of dimension.

arxiv:2611.06498.text: Signed but Steerable: Measuring and Closing the Text-Vector Integrity Gap in Offline Retrieval-Augmented Generation. From Georgios Feretzakis and colleagues. Signed knowledge packs can carry vectors that pass a signature check but misrepresent their text, letting attackers steer what an offline retrieval system finds. This work measures that gap across text collections and embedding models, and tests ways to verify stored vectors. Even tight checks can leave queries exposed, and one attack sharply reduced correct answers on a Raspberry Pi. Checking quantisation codes with a calibrated guard band accepted all honest vectors in the tested samples and prevented publishers from choosing ambiguous representations.

arxiv:2611.06346.text: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work. From Moritz Diener and colleagues. AI can improve accuracy on the job, but relying on it may deprive workers of practice and weaken skills over time. This study models how workers' skills change as they choose between solving tasks themselves and accepting AI answers. It finds that workers focused only on immediate gains can remain unskilled or lose expertise, while those who value future ability may work independently even when AI is more accurate. Incentives can help build and retain skills, and may no longer be needed once independent work becomes self-sustaining.

arxiv:2611.03771.text: ISAC-Assisted Proactive Handover in mmWave Networks: Value of Foresight and Localization Requirements. From Seyed Bagher Hashemi Natanzi and colleagues. Fast-moving blockers can disrupt millimeter-wave links before reactive handover has time to respond. This work measures the benefit of predicting future link quality and develops a system that uses communication signals to sense blockers and plan handovers. In simulated street-canyon tests, short-term perfect foresight closes most of the gap between service-aware reactive handover and an instantaneous oracle. But capturing that benefit requires localizing users and blockers to about a decimeter, far more accurately than the tested sensing provides.

arxiv:2611.06552.text: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev, Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics. From Juan José Rodríguez-Aldavero and colleagues. Global spectral solvers using compressed tensor networks have struggled with nonperiodic boundaries and with preserving the variational structure that makes these methods useful. This work builds a Chebyshev–Galerkin solver that assembles and solves boundary-value problems directly in compressed form, including variable materials, mapped shapes, and mixed boundary conditions. In a three-dimensional elasticity test, it keeps spectral accuracy and reaches errors below one hundred-millionth, outperforming the tested alternatives. It also solves over seventeen million design choices in one run and greatly reduces memory for a problem with ten random inputs.

arxiv:2611.05892.text: When Is One Query per Template Enough? Adapting Learned Cost Models to New Hardware. From Krish Patel. Moving a database to new hardware changes query runtimes by different amounts, making a model trained on the old machine unreliable. The study tests how to adapt such models using a small set of queries timed on the new hardware, across PostgreSQL workloads and several machine settings. For familiar query templates, measuring one query per template and correcting serial and parallel plans separately brings prediction error close to a model trained on the new machine. For templates not measured, corrections offer little benefit over a simple speed factor.

arxiv:2611.06382.text: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents. From Xilin Xia. Catchment models built from physical rules often lag behind neural networks, raising the question of whether simple laws can describe whole river basins. CaRT+ uses rules for water conservation, flow direction, and how unresolved catchment features affect water movement, with parameters learned separately for each basin. Across Britain and the United States, its accuracy was close to that of long short-term memory networks; in Australia, where the model had not been developed, it performed better. This suggests shared model forms can describe catchments across regions.

arxiv:2611.06888.text: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure. From Siyi Yu. Whether artificial intelligence exposure tracks work that is dull, dirty, or dangerous matters for claims that automation will ease difficult jobs. This study compares twenty-one measures of working conditions across seven hundred fifty-four United States occupations, using two exposure measures and both equal and employment-based weighting. Higher exposure is linked to lower scores for these conditions, but adjustment weakens the overall link; it remains negative for one measure and becomes uncertain for the other. The findings show that how conditions are grouped and which job traits are considered can change what exposure estimates mean.

arxiv:2611.05831.text: Functional inequalities from the fundamental limits of Bayesian estimation. From Shuchen Li and colleagues. Functional inequalities describe how the shape of a probability distribution limits variation and information. This work connects these inequalities for log-concave measures to lower bounds on how well one can estimate a hidden quantity from a noisy observation. Using that connection, it gives an information-based proof that the Poincaré constant grows at most as the square root of the dimension. For smooth subgaussian measures, it also improves the known log-Sobolev bound to grow only as the fourth root of the dimension.

arxiv:2611.06504.text: NaijaFacts: A Framework for Disentangling Language from Knowledge in Facts about Nigeria. From Zainab Afolabi and colleagues. Most multilingual tests check whether models can understand local languages, not whether they know facts about Africa. NaijaFacts tests factual and statistical knowledge about Nigeria with questions written by native speakers in five languages, then compares answers with similar questions about the United Kingdom and the United States. Across eight models, missing knowledge mattered more than language: accuracy was 20 percent on Nigerian questions in English, versus 49 to 50 percent for the other countries. The same gap appeared across Africa, especially for statistics.
